procedural_history.originating_court: Court of judicial magistrate, F.C. Shahada, Nandurbar District
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 02.07.2018 of the High Court of Judicature at Bombay, Bench at Aurangabad in Criminal Application No. 3590 of 2012.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant filed a criminal application under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 before the High Court for quashing the FIR No.59 of 2000 and the chargesheet. The High Court dismissed the criminal petition by its order dated 02.07.2018.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant approached the Supreme Court after the High Court dismissed his application to quash the FIR and chargesheet. The Supreme Court granted leave to appeal and allowed the appeal, implying a reversal of the High Court's decision.

directions: The impugned order of the High Court dated 02.07.2018 in Criminal Application No.3590 of 2012, is hereby set aside.

The First Information Report dated 6.12.2000 filed by the complainant in the Police Station at Mhasawad, District Nandurbar, on the basis of which Crime No.59 of 2000 is registered against the appellant, is hereby quashed.

The chargesheet dated 14.06.2001 filed by Mhasawad Police Station against the appellant for the offences under Sections 376 (2)(b), 420 read with Section 34 of the IPC and Section 3(1)(x) of the SC/ST Act is also quashed.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court can quash criminal proceedings under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C. if the allegations in the complaint do not constitute an offence or if their continuance amounts to an abuse of the process of the court.

facts: An FIR was registered against the appellant (a doctor) by the complainant (a nurse) under sections for rape, cheating, and offenses under the SC/ST Act.
The complaint arose after a consensual relationship between the two ended when the appellant married another woman.
The appellant filed a petition in the High Court under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C. to quash the FIR, but the High Court dismissed it.
The appellant then appealed this dismissal to the Supreme Court.
law: The High Court has inherent power under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C. to quash proceedings to prevent the abuse of the process of any court or to secure the ends of justice.
This power is an exception, not the rule, and must be exercised sparingly and with caution.
The High Court is justified in quashing a proceeding if its initiation or continuance amounts to an abuse of the court's process.

Specifically, if the allegations set out in the complaint, even when accepted in their entirety, do not constitute the offense of which cognizance has been taken, it is open to the High Court to quash the proceedings.
In exercising this power, the court should not conduct a meticulous analysis or appreciation of evidence as a trial court would.
application: The Supreme Court examined the allegations in the FIR at face value.
It noted that the physical relationship was admittedly consensual, which means the facts did not constitute an offense of rape under Section 376, IPC.
The Court also found that the FIR did not contain any allegations that would make out a case for cheating under Section 420, IPC, or an offense under the SC/ST Act.

Because the allegations, even if accepted as true, did not make out a case against the appellant for the charged offenses, the Court determined that the continuation of the criminal proceeding was manifestly attended with mala fides and was an abuse of the process of the court.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court can and should quash criminal proceedings under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C. if the allegations in the complaint do not constitute an offense or if their continuance amounts to an abuse of the court's process. Therefore, the Supreme Court held that the High Court was not justified in rejecting the appellant's petition and proceeded to quash the FIR.

issue.issue_text: Whether the complaint registered under Section 376(2)(b) of the IPC can be sustained when the complainant has failed to prima facie show the commission of rape.

facts: The appellant was a government doctor and the complainant was a nurse at the same establishment.
The complainant, a widow, stated she had fallen in love with the appellant and needed a companion.
They were in a consensual relationship for a significant time, living together intermittently at both of their residences.
The appellant had promised to marry her.
The complainant filed an FIR for rape after she discovered that the appellant had married another woman.
It was not the complainant's case that the appellant had forcibly raped her; the physical relationship was acknowledged as consensual.
law: The court draws a clear distinction between rape and consensual sex.
There is a legal difference between a "mere breach of a promise" to marry and a "false promise" made with the sole malicious intention to seduce a woman for sexual acts.

For a sexual act to be considered rape, the consent must have been given under a "misconception of fact." If a woman consents to sexual intercourse due to her love and passion for the accused, and not solely because of the promise to marry, it does not amount to rape.
An acknowledged consensual physical relationship does not constitute an offence under Section 376 of the IPC.
application: The Court found that the relationship was based on mutual affection, as the complainant herself stated she was in love and needed a companion.

It determined that the complainant's consent was a "conscious decision" and not the result of a misconception created by the appellant's promise. Her consent was tacit and not given under psychological pressure.
The Court viewed the situation as a "breach of a promise" rather than a "false promise" made with the sole intent to deceive for sexual gratification from the beginning.
Based on these factors, the Court concluded that even if all the allegations in the complaint were taken at face value, they did not establish a prima facie case for the offence of rape.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that since the complainant failed to prima facie show the commission of rape, as the relationship was long-term and consensual, and her consent was based on love and not solely on a false promise, the complaint under Section 376(2)(b) of the IPC could not be sustained and was therefore quashed.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court can quash criminal proceedings under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C. if the allegations in the complaint do not constitute an offence or if their continuance amounts to an abuse of the process of the court.
appellant_arguments: The process of the court was being abused by the complainant with an oblique motive.
The criminal proceeding was manifestly intended with mala fides and maliciously instituted with an ulterior motive.
Even if the entire allegations in the complaint are taken at face value and accepted in their entirety, they do not constitute any offence.
The complainant was constantly blackmailing the appellant.
respondent_arguments: The respondent sought to justify the impugned order of the High Court, which had declined to quash the proceedings.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the complaint registered under Section 376(2)(b) of the IPC can be sustained when the complainant has failed to prima facie show the commission of rape.
appellant_arguments: The allegations made in the complaint, even if accepted in their entirety, do not constitute an offence.
The complainant was in a relationship with and married the appellant's brother, not the appellant.
The complaint was maliciously instituted with an ulterior motive as the complainant was blackmailing the appellant.
respondent_arguments: The respondent sought to justify the High Court's order, implying that the complaint should be sustained and that a prima facie case was made out.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The High Court's inherent powers under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C. are to be exercised as an exception, not the rule, to prevent the abuse of the process of any court or to secure the ends of justice. This jurisdiction is not unlimited and must be exercised in accordance with the law, including procedural law.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Supreme Court found that the High Court should have exercised its jurisdiction under Section 482 Cr.P.C. to quash the criminal proceedings, as their continuance constituted an abuse of the process of the court. The Court determined that the proceeding was manifestly attended with mala fides and maliciously instituted with an ulterior motive, and that the judicial process, being a solemn proceeding, cannot be allowed to be converted into an instrument of oppression or harassment.
legal_tests_applied: The inherent power of the High Court under Section 482 Cr.P.C. can be exercised to prevent the abuse of the process of any court or to secure the ends of justice.

The test from State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal, specifically the categories where: (3) the uncontroverted allegations in the FIR or complaint do not disclose the commission of any offence; and (7) a criminal proceeding is manifestly attended with mala fides and/or maliciously instituted with an ulterior motive.

When a complaint is sought to be quashed, it is permissible for the court to examine the materials to assess the allegations and determine if an offence is made out, even if the allegations are accepted in toto.
The High Court has a duty to thwart attempts to abuse the solemn process of the court with some oblique motive at the very threshold.
policy_considerations: It would be an abuse of process of the court to allow any action which would result in injustice and prevent promotion of justice.
The inherent power given to the High Court under Section 482 Cr.P.C. is with the purpose and object of advancement of justice.
Judicial process is a solemn proceeding which cannot be allowed to be converted into an instrument of oppression or harassment.
In case the solemn process of Court is sought to be abused by a person with some oblique motive, the Court has to thwart the attempt at the very threshold.
